name: Leg Recovery to De La Riva
description: Master Leg Recovery to De La Riva from leg drag bottom. Extract trapped leg, insert DLR hook to re-establish guard. Success rates: Beginner 30%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 65%.
overview:
Leg Recovery to De La Riva represents a critical defensive transition for practitioners caught in the compromised leg drag control position. When your opponent has successfully dragged your leg across your body and is threatening to advance to side control or take your back, this technique provides a pathway to re-establish an offensive guard position rather than merely surviving.

The fundamental challenge of leg drag recovery lies in the mechanical disadvantage created by the crossed leg configuration. Your trapped leg cannot simply be pulled back—it requires specific angles, timing, and coordinated movement to extract. The De La Riva hook insertion transforms what would be a desperate scramble into a calculated guard recovery that immediately puts you back on offense.

Strategically, this transition exploits a fundamental vulnerability in the leg drag position: the opponent must maintain forward pressure while controlling both your leg and upper body. When they adjust their weight or reach for new grips, windows open for leg extraction. The key insight is recognizing that you are not escaping to a neutral position—you are transitioning directly to an attacking guard that gives you immediate sweep and submission threats. This mindset shift from defense to offense is what separates successful recoveries from those that merely delay the inevitable pass.
key_principles: Create frames at shoulder and hip before attempting leg extraction
Use hip movement to create angle rather than pulling leg directly back
Insert DLR hook immediately upon leg extraction to prevent re-drag
Time extraction to opponent's weight shifts or grip adjustments
Maintain collar or sleeve grip throughout transition to establish guard attacks
Never turn away from opponent during extraction—stay facing them
setup_requirements: Opponent has established leg drag control with your leg crossed over your body
You have created at least one frame against opponent's shoulder or hip
Your free leg has mobility to assist extraction or block opponent's advance
Opponent's weight is distributed enough to allow hip movement

execution_steps.description: Place your near-side hand on opponent's shoulder or bicep, creating a stiff arm frame. Your far-side hand controls their sleeve or collar to prevent them from settling weight or establishing crossface.
execution_steps.timing: Immediately upon recognizing leg drag position

execution_steps.description: Perform a hip escape away from opponent while keeping your shoulders relatively flat. This creates space between your hip and their controlling pressure without exposing your back.
execution_steps.timing: When opponent shifts weight or reaches for new grip

execution_steps.description: Use your free leg to push against opponent's hip or hook behind their knee. This creates additional space and prevents them from following your hip escape with forward pressure.
Pull your trapped leg back by driving your knee toward your chest in a circular motion, not straight back. The angle created by your hip escape allows the leg to clear their grip and body.
execution_steps.timing: As space is created from steps 2-3

execution_steps.description: Immediately thread your extracted leg around opponent's front leg, placing your foot behind their knee or thigh to establish the De La Riva hook. Your instep hooks their inner thigh.
execution_steps.timing: Within one second of leg extraction

execution_steps.description: Secure collar and sleeve grips appropriate for De La Riva attacks. Your non-hooking leg establishes contact on their hip or sleeve-controlled arm. Begin off-balancing immediately.

common_counters.counter: Opponent drives forward and re-establishes heavy shoulder pressure before you can extract
common_counters.your_response: Maintain frames and wait for next weight shift; do not force extraction against settled pressure

common_counters.counter: Opponent releases leg drag to backstep into leg entanglement as you extract
common_counters.your_response: Immediately pummel your free leg inside to prevent ashi garami entry and sit up to address the leg attack

common_counters.counter: Opponent transitions to knee slice as your leg comes free
common_counters.your_response: Use extracted leg to establish knee shield before they can complete the slice; DLR hook prevents their hip from advancing

common_counters.counter: Opponent releases upper body control to re-drag your leg before hook is established
common_counters.your_response: Use the momentary lack of upper body control to sit up and face them, establishing open guard

common_errors.error: Pulling trapped leg straight back without creating angle first
common_errors.consequence: Leg remains stuck against opponent's grip and body weight, wasting energy
common_errors.correction: Hip escape to create angle before attempting extraction; the leg must travel in an arc, not a straight line

common_errors.error: Turning away from opponent to extract leg, exposing back
common_errors.consequence: Opponent follows the rotation and takes back control instead of leg drag
common_errors.correction: Keep shoulders relatively square throughout; create space with hip movement while maintaining chest orientation

common_errors.error: Failing to insert DLR hook immediately after leg extraction
common_errors.consequence: Opponent re-drags the leg or transitions to another pass before guard is established
common_errors.correction: Treat leg extraction and hook insertion as a single continuous motion; the hook is the finish, not the extraction

common_errors.error: Attempting extraction while opponent has full weight settled
common_errors.consequence: Technique fails and you exhaust yourself fighting settled pressure
common_errors.correction: Wait for opponent to adjust position, reach for grip, or shift weight before initiating extraction sequence

common_errors.error: Neglecting upper body grips during transition
common_errors.consequence: Successfully establish DLR but opponent immediately passes or disengages the hook
common_errors.correction: Maintain at least one controlling grip throughout; secure full guard grips within two seconds of hook insertion

training_progressions.description: Practice the hip escape to angle and leg extraction sequence against a stationary partner. Focus on the circular path of leg extraction and immediate hook insertion. Partner provides position but no resistance.

Partner provides light pressure in leg drag and makes small weight shifts or grip adjustments. Bottom player identifies windows and executes extraction during these moments. Develop sensitivity to weight distribution.

Chain the DLR recovery with immediate attacks: sweeps, berimbolo entries, back takes. If recovery fails, transition to alternative escapes like technical standup or turtle. Build a complete defensive flowchart.

Full resistance guard passing rounds where partner actively attempts leg drag passes. Implement recovery in real time against opponents using counter-techniques and transitions. Stress-test timing and execution under pressure.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Instead of inserting a standard DLR hook, thread your leg to the outside and establish Reverse De La Riva. Particularly effective when opponent's stance is square or when they begin retreating.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent backs away during your extraction or has a very upright posture

variants_and_adaptations.description: As you extract your leg, immediately hook your instep behind their knee and establish your other leg on their hip for Single Leg X guard. This captures their leg and creates immediate sweep threats.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent drops their weight low during your extraction or when they step their dragging leg forward

variants_and_adaptations.description: During extraction, thread your outside leg across their body and establish K-Guard configuration. Requires more hip mobility but provides strong leg entanglement entries.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When you have strong hip flexibility and want to threaten leg locks immediately upon recovery

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the primary goal of Leg Recovery to De La Riva?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary goal is to transform a defensive, compromised position into an offensive guard where you have immediate sweep and submission threats. Rather than simply escaping to neutral or surviving, you are establishing De La Riva guard which gives you back the initiative.

knowledge_assessment.question: What position do you start Leg Recovery to De La Riva from?
knowledge_assessment.answer: This technique starts from Leg Drag Control Bottom, where your opponent has pulled one of your legs across your body and is using it to control your hips while threatening to advance to side control, mount, or back control.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the key grips needed for Leg Recovery to De La Riva?
knowledge_assessment.answer: During extraction, you need a frame grip on the opponent's shoulder or bicep to create distance, plus a sleeve or collar grip to prevent them from settling weight. Upon establishing DLR, you need a collar grip and sleeve grip to control their posture and near arm for sweeps and attacks.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent maintains heavy shoulder pressure and won't shift their weight—how do you create an extraction window?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Use your free leg to push against their hip or hook behind their knee, forcing them to adjust their base. Alternatively, threaten with your collar grip or attempt to sit up, which forces them to address the upper body threat and momentarily reduces pressure on your trapped leg. Never force extraction against settled pressure.

knowledge_assessment.question: When is the best time to attempt Leg Recovery to De La Riva?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The optimal window is when your opponent shifts their weight to reach for a new grip, adjusts their position to advance, or transitions toward another passing option. These moments create brief reductions in pressure on your trapped leg. Attempting against fully settled weight wastes energy and typically fails.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why must the DLR hook be inserted immediately upon leg extraction?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The moment your leg is free, your opponent will attempt to re-drag it or transition to another pass. The DLR hook must be inserted within one second of extraction to prevent this. The hook creates a structural barrier that prevents them from re-establishing leg drag and immediately threatens their base.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent backsteps toward leg entanglement as you extract your leg—what is your response?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Immediately pummel your free leg to the inside to prevent them from securing inside ashi garami or saddle position. Sit up aggressively and face them to address the leg attack. If they already have leg entanglement, fight for inside position on your captured leg and work standard leg lock defense sequences.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the critical difference in hip movement between a failed and successful leg extraction?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Failed extractions attempt to pull the leg straight back against the opponent's grip and body weight. Successful extractions use hip escape to create an angle first, then extract the leg in a circular arc toward the chest. The angle created by the hip escape allows the leg to clear the controlling pressure that would otherwise block direct extraction.

safety_considerations: Leg Recovery to De La Riva is generally a low-risk defensive transition with minimal injury potential when executed properly. The primary safety concern is avoiding the temptation to forcefully yank your trapped leg free, which can strain hip flexors or groin muscles if the opponent maintains strong control. Always create space through proper technique before extracting. During training, partners should provide progressive resistance and immediately release control if the bottom player signals discomfort. Be mindful of knee torque on the hooking leg once DLR is established—ensure the hook is placed correctly behind the knee or thigh rather than on the knee joint itself.
position_integration: Leg Recovery to De La Riva fits within the broader guard retention and recovery system as a proactive defensive option from one of the most common modern passing positions. The leg drag has become a staple of high-level guard passing, making proficiency in this recovery essential. Once established in De La Riva, you have access to the complete DLR attack system: sweeps like the basic DLR sweep and berimbolo, back takes, and transitions to other guards like X-Guard or Single Leg X. This technique connects your defensive game to your offensive guard game, ensuring that surviving a pass attempt immediately returns you to a threatening position rather than a neutral scramble. Practitioners should drill this alongside other leg drag escapes (technical standup, turtle transition, half guard recovery) to develop a complete defensive flowchart.
